topic: Eigenvectors: the directions a matrix only stretches

segments.narration: What if a matrix could move every vector, except a special few?
segments.visual: Title 'Eigenvectors' with the subtitle 'the arrows a matrix can't turn'

segments.narration: This matrix transforms the whole plane. Apply it, and every vector gets pushed somewhere new.
segments.visual: The matrix A = [[2,1],[1,2]] above a small coordinate grid

segments.narration: Watch these two arrows: they swing around to point in completely new directions.
segments.visual: Two grey arrows on the grid rotate to their transformed positions

segments.narration: But this arrow never turns. The matrix only stretches it along its own line.
segments.visual: A blue arrow on the diagonal stretches to three times its length along a dashed line

segments.narration: Any vector like this is called an eigenvector: A times v equals lambda times v.
segments.visual: The equation A v = lambda v appears below the grid

segments.narration: Lambda is the eigenvalue, the stretch factor. Here the arrow tripled, so lambda is three.
segments.visual: The equation becomes A v = 3 v and the blue arrow flashes

segments.narration: Eigenvectors are the directions a matrix treats as its own: it scales them, and does nothing more.
segments.visual: Everything fades except the payoff line 'the directions a matrix only scales'
